All digital · nothing built yet

IEEE SoutheastCon 2027 · Hardware competition · Daytona Beach · Apr 17

The stock carrace robot

An all-digital design, physics and simulation package for the 2027 Stock Car Race: the organizer's own CAD field, a vendor-CAD-verified drivetrain mule, motor-physics speed limits, and 91 of 91 simulated full missions finishing and parking — built to become a team baseline, not a trophy claim.

  • 91 / 91sim missions finished & parked
  • 390 ptsV3.0 robot score modeled
  • 21–24 in/smodel top speed
  • 0 partsordered — that is the ask
  • Apr 17 '27three quals, best one counts
Personal hobby & learning project · most analysis and code produced with AI assistance (agent-run) · physical work is claimed only when the owner records measurements · nothing here is a validated competition robot.

The race in 20 seconds

Start on the green flag, run 3 laps around the oval dodging 3 toy-vehicle obstacles, detour to your assigned pit box after lap 2 for a tire exchange, finish the victory lap and park. Score model: 390 robot points + 10 publicity. Under 2:45 earns a 30-point speed bonus.

Rules V3.0 V3.1 start-flag appendix pending

01 — The arena

Every dimension from the organizer's own CAD

The field is a 4 × 8 ft sheet with 4 in walls, a 36 in center divider splitting the oval, and a pit end with three 12 × 12 in boxes. Below is not traced from a drawing photo — the arena geometry was extracted from the organizer's June 2026 Fusion 360 file (B-rep parsed, hashed and cross-checked against the V3 drawing, in derived/organizer-cad-v10/).

walls track marking (≈0.9 in band) dividers obstacle quadrants checker = start/finish start box

Source: organizer Fusion 360 arena file, B-rep dated Jun 14 2026, extracted and hashed in derived/organizer-cad-v10/. Nominal CAD values — the built field may vary by ±1 in (GM2 G02). Pinch points are real: the race-end strip between marking and wall is only 6.995 in, narrower than the 10 in minimum robot.

FIELD FINDING

Obstacle size decides the 75 obstacle points

Using the organizer guide's plush vehicle (≈8.55 × 8.2 in) on the CAD field, a 10 in robot can pass one without contact in only 0–47% of placements — and a full three-obstacle lap is contact-free in just 0–2.5% of random layouts. If the official toy set is that size, a gentle-contact policy beats dodging. Measuring the real vehicles (official list, $35.95) is the highest-value physical test.

RULES MODEL

390 robot points + 10 publicity

V3.0 scoring: three laps (100), enter course (25), green-flag start (10), no wall contact (15/lap), no obstacle contact (25/lap), exchange (40 + 25), finish under 3:00 (100), speed bonus (30), park in box (15), school flag (25). Ten rule questions are drafted and ready for the official Discord Q&A.

02 — The car & the parts

A test mule first — with two vendor-CAD catches before anything was printed

The first build is deliberately a drivetrain mule (a rolling test rig, not the competition chassis): two Pololu 70:1 37D gearmotors with encoders on a printed deck. Before ordering or printing a single part, the whole stack was modeled against Pololu's own STEP files — which caught two errors that a paper design would have missed.

The catch (CAD measurements, not received parts)

Pololu's gearmotor output shaft sits 7 mm off the gearbox center, and the original mule kit's deck, built as drawn, would have left the wheels 7.09 mm off the floor and the casters rocking 1.08 mm. The corrected v10 deck flips the motors shaft-down, adds printed 6.91 mm caster risers, and ships with a true-scale drill template plus STEP/STL regenerated from caliper-checked dimensions. derived/drivetrain-mule-v10/

Integrated workspace · assembly sequence + live contact simulation

From loose parts to a working digital robot.

One document, no separate studio file needed. The sequence seats the deck, motors, wheels, casters, proposed lift and generic battery/controller reservations, then starts the live mission. Purchased-part shapes are editable CadQuery exterior studies—not exact product replicas. Click a component to inspect what is documented and what is still approximate.

Live demonstration arena: 4.86 × 2.48 m, enlarged for maneuvering. Miniature couches are stress-test props, not official competition obstacles. The planner uses known obstacle positions; this is not camera perception. Three laps are counted from ordered position gates. Contacts may cause bumps, stalls, a dropped tire, or a failed mission.

Select historical simulated mission to inspect the event sequence.


Evidence boundary: LIVE uses Rapier rigid-body contacts for the tire, fixtures, tray and obstacles, with a force-driven chassis constrained to a level plane and a position-controlled lift. No tire parenting, pickup weld or timer-declared acquisition is used. Chassis tipping, individual wheel suspension, motor electrical dynamics, lift compliance and perception are not modeled. The amber lift/tray is a proposed custom mechanism, not purchased hardware. Historical replay remains a separate timer-driven Python trace on the competition field and does not validate this new assembly. All runs are agent-authored digital studies; no physical robot or owner-reviewed qualification is claimed.





  

    
03 — Physics

    
What the drivetrain model says the car can actually do

    
A motor-physics model (torque-speed curve, grip limit, battery sag, 0.42 ms physics substeps, corrected against hand calculations) replaces guessed speed limits. Agent-run sim Placeholder friction 0.15–0.35 Not measurements

    

      

        
FINDING 01

        
The outer wheel is the speed limit

        1.53×
        
On a 7.5 in U-turn the outer wheel runs 1.53× the robot's center speed. Model top speed is 21.0–24.3 in/s, but keeping wheel headroom caps the cruise at 12 in/s (outer wheel 18.4 in/s, 88% of the lowest top speed). 16 in/s would need 24.5 in/s at the wheel — undrivable through the U-turns.

      

      

        
FINDING 02

        
Grip, not the motors, limits accel

        0.27 N·m
        
Each wheel can transmit ≈ 0.27 N·m before slipping (μ 0.35, 5 kg) against the motor's 2.65 N·m extrapolated stall. The 70:1 motors are fine; floor friction is the number the design most needs, and the E03 floor trials are set up to measure exactly that.

      

      

        
FINDING 03

        
Plan for peak current

        6 A+
        
Drive energy is tiny (0.04–0.05 Wh per mission) and cruise is ≈ 0.31 A, but full-command spins hit the assumed 3 A per-motor limit. Size the fuse and battery wiring for 6 A plus electronics; battery choice is set by peak current, sag and swap speed — not capacity.

04 — Simulation

    
91 of 91 simulated full missions finished and parked

    
Whole missions chain the pieces a real robot would run: supervisor and mission driver, route files, path tracker, pose estimator, and the firmware's closed-loop wheel control against the corrected drivetrain model — on the organizer-CAD field, across four evaluation sets with randomized layouts.

    
    

    

      
SetMissionsFinished & parkedWall contactsVehicle contactsMedian finishScore-like

      
        
clean (no obstacles)2727 / 270058.2 s390

        
vehicles (guide-size obstacles)2020 / 20060 laps touched58.8 s285.8

        
library (route-library paths)3232 / 320063.4 s390

        
paths (alternate routes)1212 / 120062.9 s357.5

      
    

    

    
Read this honestly: "score-like" is an event tally, not a score prediction. Median finishes (≈ 58–63 s) are far inside the 2:45 speed-bonus line — but the camera, start flag and lap line are not modeled, and a touched vehicle neither resists nor moves. The tightest moment in every run is a square base spinning in the pit box: 0.27–0.61 in from the wall.

    

      
Also in the loop: localization & the fallback

      
In simulation, cheap low-range sensors plus gyro and encoders keep the pose within ≈ 1 in of truth through a whole mission; a reflectance-only fallback also finishes, which matters if the camera struggles with glare on real paint. Glare over 5–10% of the AprilTag (tagStandard41h12, IDs 1–3) broke single-frame decoding in tests, so the detector votes over several frames.

    

  






  

    
05 — Honest limits

    
What this is not

    

      
    
        
  • Nothing is physical. No parts ordered, no field built, no bench or floor trials, no robot. The mule deck is drawn, not printed.
    • 
        
  • Parameters are placeholders. Friction (0.15–0.35), mass, inertia and battery resistance await E02 bench and E03 floor measurements.
    • 
        
  • Camera, flag and lap line are not modeled. Tag and flag events are simply given to the software.
    • 
        
  • Vehicles are ghosts. A touched obstacle neither resists nor moves, so contact behavior is unknown until real-set trials.
    • 
        
  • No trained policy. The RL interface exists but no learning is planned before real sensor data (and none is claimed).
    • 
        
  • Field geometry is nominal CAD (June 2026, pre-V3) and the built field may vary ±1 in per element.
    • 
        
  • Agent-run ≠ qualified. Simulations are leads to check, not measurements; earlier overclaims (e.g. "20/20 episodes") were corrected in ERRATA-2026-11.md.
    • 
        
  • Rule questions are open. Ten are drafted for the official Discord Q&A; none is posted, and official answers can change legal routes.
    • 
      

    

  






  

    
06 — Next

    
From digital to physical: the next four moves

    
Everything above exists to de-risk the first purchases and the first build weekend. The gate plan targets a concept design review by Dec 13, 2026, a fabrication release Jan 10, and a full practice field well before the Feb reliability campaign.

    

      
MOVE 01
Post the rule questions
Ten Q&A items are drafted with manual references (envelope & round base, tag location, obstacle vehicles and placement, track-marking legality, pit access, lap counting, exchange & parking, start flag, field tolerances, publicity). The official Discord Q&A outranks the manuals — answers reshape the concept.

      
MOVE 02
Order A: the drivetrain
$177.25 researched (motors, brackets, hubs, wheels, casters). On arrival: caliper-check against the inspection templates, then print the corrected mule deck. This is the first physical evidence in the whole project.

      
MOVE 03
Build the practice field
Materials from the organizer's own list ($182.39 including paint, start flag and the official obstacle set; brushes/tape under $35). Build it, then measure it as built — the ±1 in tolerance is a designed-in variation the robot must survive.

      
MOVE 04
Measure, then re-baseline
Bench characterization (E02) and floor trials (E03) replace the placeholder friction and motor values; tire-replica pickup tests pick the exchange mechanism. Every measurement flows back into the simulator and the CAD.

AI assistance: AI coding assistants, including Claude (Anthropic), produced most of the analysis, software and documentation across many sessions; an October 2026 drawing transcription used a panel of vision models. Nothing in this showcase is a validated competition robot.

Assumptions, attribution and limits
A digital study, not a hardware certificate.
1.35 kg rounded whole-chassis assumption. Motor mass 205 g each is archived manufacturer data; remaining allocations are estimates, not measured values. No hardware purchased.
  • Level-plane chassis cannot tip; tire is fully dynamic
  • Force-limited virtual wheel traction, not individual rolling wheel bodies
  • Ideal position-controlled lift with payload-weight gating, not torque/compliance simulation
  • Known-map navigation; no camera, lidar, flag detector or firmware controller parity
  • New enlarged demo arena is not competition geometry or a scoring qualification
  • Tray and fixture geometry proposed for this demo, not measured organizer hardware
  • 22 mm archived motor CAD shaft datum versus 16 mm published length remains unresolved
  • No transferred historical 91/91 results; parameter changes require a new live run
  • Couches are fictional miniature demo props; not official competition obstacles
